newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: FOCUS-Australia inflation low boosts rate cut talk.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Australia inflation low boosts rate cut talk.

text.p: Australia announced record low inflation on Wednesday, increasing the chances of another interest rate cut to promote growth and cut unemployment.

The Consumer Price Index (CPI) for the June quarter fell by 0.2 percent for an annual rise of 0.3 percent, the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) reported. It was the first quarter of headline deflation since June 1992.
Underlying inflation fell to an annual 1.7 percent, its lowest rate since records began in 1971.
Underlying inflation for the quarter was 0.3 percent.

Australian Treasurer Peter Costello -- whose efforts to jumpstart the economy have been foiled by a stubborn lack of consumer and business confidence -- welcomed the CPI data as "an exceptionally good result".

"This all adds up to a very good climate for investment: historically low inflation, historically low interest rates, a budget which is on track to put the Commonwealth (Australian government) into a position where it will be a saver," Costello told a news conference in Melbourne.
"It will keep the pressure off interest rates and as a consequence it is a very, very good investment climate through 1997 and 1998," Costello said.

The ABS is due on Thursday to announce May quarter weekly wages data and economists said moderate figures could persuade the Reserve Bank of Australia to cut interest rates for the fifth time in a year. A cut could come as early as Friday.

Underlying inflation, which excludes items that are highly volatile or follow seasonal patterns, is now below the Reserve Bank's own annual target band of two to three percent, allowing it more flexibility on official interest rates.

The previous four RBA cuts in the current cycle, each of 50 basis points taking the official cash rate to 5.5 percent, have so far failed to work their way through to increased economic confidence and activity.
Retail sales have remained sluggish and unemployment has remained stuck at or above 8.5 percent.
Economists pointed out that comments by U.S. Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan overnight appeared to have relieved pressure for a hike in U.S. interest rates.
"It's a splendid result and we think it meets the second of three conditions for a rate cut to be announced on Friday," said John Edwards, chief economist at HSBC Markets.

"The other one was the confirmed reluctance of the Federal Reserve to raise rates and the next condition is tomorrow's average weekly earnings which in our view have to display moderate overall earnings growth to permit another rate cut."
The Australian dollar eased slightly and bonds jumped after the inflation report, although the dollar soon picked up lost ground and the bond rally quickly hit profit-taking.
Economists said another rate cut was already largely factored into market prices.
A fifth cut could, however, hit offshore sentiment because Australian rates would be lower than U.S. rates, threatening the Aussie dollar's traditional high-yielder status.

In a statement, Costello said the recent fall in the value of the Australian dollar could put modest upward pressure on underlying inflation. The A$ has fallen by four U.S. cents since the last reduction in official interest rates on May 23.
